story_text: The moon had climbed high enough to reach the tall windows, and the whole library had turned silver. Yasmin stood in the middle of it with her hands pressed flat against her coat, listening. Nothing creaked. Nothing rustled. Even the dust hung in the air as if it were waiting for her to say something first. Every instinct told her to run. The great door was only a few dozen steps away, and beyond it lay the cool night and the quiet street. She could be outside in a moment, breathing hard and telling herself that the whole thing had been a strange dream. Her feet had already turned halfway toward the exit. Then she stopped. “If I leave,” she whispered, “the questions will still be here when I come back. They just won't be any smaller.” Her own voice sounded thin in all that space, but saying it aloud made it true. She let out a long breath and turned back to the shelves. The moonlight lay in long pale bands across the floor, and as the minutes passed the bands slid slowly along the rows of books, touching one spine and then the next, like a patient finger reading a very long page. Yasmin watched it move and tried to think clearly. Something should have ended tonight. That was what she had expected. The work was supposed to be finished, the last promise kept, the great door closed behind her with a satisfying click. But nothing had ended. The Agreement she had given her word to was still open. She could feel it the way you feel a forgotten errand sitting at the back of your mind. She walked to the nearest reading table and rested her fingertips on the cold wood. “Why is nothing finished?” she asked the room. The room, of course, did not answer. But the silence did not feel empty. It felt like the silence of someone who is waiting for you to notice the obvious. The obvious was this: the Agreement had not closed. No one else was here to finish it. If the work was unfinished, then the work belonged to her, and it would go on belonging to her whether she stayed or fled. Yasmin straightened her shoulders. It was a heavy thing to understand, but it was oddly steadying too, like finding the floor in the dark. “All right,” she said. “Then I'll look.” She began to walk the length of the nearest aisle, slowly, letting the moonlight show her the way. Her search had a shape now, and the shape was a question she could not yet answer. There was an atlas, and she did not know who it belonged to. That was the second thing that stayed open. She had no name for the owner and no hint of where the atlas might be. She only knew that the Agreement and the atlas were tied together, and that the knot would not loosen on its own. So she started with what she knew. The library was the one place she had learned by heart, or most of it. She knew the corner where the floorboards sang if you stepped on the third plank. She knew the long window seat with its faded cushion, the spiral stair that led to the gallery, and the low cabinet of maps that stuck whenever the weather turned damp. She went to each of them in turn, and she looked the way a careful person looks, not the way a hopeful person does. At the window seat she lifted the cushion and found only a pale square where the sun had never faded the wood. At the singing plank she knelt and ran her fingers along the gaps, but there was only dust, soft and gray and old. She climbed the spiral stair, her shoes ringing softly on the iron, and walked the gallery rail from one end to the other. Below her the library lay spread out in light and shadow, and she searched every shelf she could see for a gap, a mark, a note, a name. She found nothing that said whose atlas it was. At the map cabinet she tugged the stubborn drawers one by one. Some held rolled sheets of coastlines she did not recognize. Some held only empty paper. None carried a signature, a stamp, or a scribbled initial. It would have been easy, then, to decide. A tidy answer was right there, waiting to be picked up like a coin. She could say the atlas belonged to the library itself, or to some old keeper whose name she half-remembered, or to whoever had last sat at the big table. Any of those would have let her stop searching and feel finished. Yasmin sat down on the bottom step of the spiral stair and stared at the idea for a while. “I could say it,” she murmured. “It would sound sensible.” But sensible was not the same as true. If she handed herself a false answer, she would build everything after it on sand, and she would never know which parts were real. So she shook her head. “I don't know whose it is,” she said, very plainly. “I don't know. And that's all right. It just means I'm not done.” The words did not make her feel small. They made her feel clean, as if a window inside her had been wiped. And with that cleaner view came a quiet certainty: she had searched the library she knew, and the library had nothing more to tell her. Whatever answers there were, they were not in these corners. She tilted her head back and looked at the tall windows. Through the farthest one, past the black outline of rooftops, the moon lit something she had never really looked at before. It was a tall, narrow shape against the sky, standing alone. A tower. She had heard that word before. She had never gone near it. It lay beyond everything she had ever needed to see, and until tonight she had never wondered what it was. Now she wondered very much. She did not know what she would find there. She did not even know that the tower held an answer. But the library had run out of places to look, and the tower was the nearest place she had not looked at all. “So that's where I go,” she said. Her heart gave a nervous little thump, because the library was the one safe place she truly knew. Leaving it felt like stepping off the last stair in the dark. Still, she thought of the door behind her and of the long road she would walk, and she told herself something firmly: she could always come back. The library would be here. The moonlight would still be crossing the floor. Going did not mean being lost. Yasmin pulled her coat tighter, crossed the silver floor, and pushed open the great door. The night air met her like cool water. She stepped out, closed the door gently behind her, and set off toward the tower. The road was quiet. The moon rode along above her, patient and round, and her shadow stretched ahead of her on the stones, long and thin and a little brave. Time moved with her step by step. At first the tower was only a dark finger over the rooftops. Then the rooftops thinned, and the finger grew taller, until it filled a good part of the sky. She slowed at the last bend, partly from tiredness and partly from nerves. Then she stepped out from the shadow of a wall, and there it was. The tower rose from a patch of rough ground, built of pale stone that the moonlight had turned the color of milk. It was far taller than it had looked from the library window. Narrow windows climbed its side in a slow spiral, and at the top a ring of stone teeth stood against the stars. Yasmin walked right up to it and stopped a little way from the base, with her neck tilted back and her mouth slightly open. “It's real,” she said. It was a silly thing to say, but it was the first true thing she had to give. All her life the tower had been a rumor, a shape at the edge of her thinking. Now she could see the seams between its stones and feel the cold breath of it on her face. She made herself slow down and look carefully, the way she had looked in the library. This time she was determined to keep two lists in her mind: what she could actually see, and what she only wanted to be there. In the first list went the stone, rough under her palm when she reached out and touched it. In went the door at the base, tall and arched, shut tight, with a dark iron ring for a handle. In went the windows above, every one of them dark, and the worn steps leading up to the threshold, hollowed in the middle by many feet over many years. She counted the windows she could see and got eleven, and decided that eleven was a fact. In the second list went all the things her imagination kept offering her. It whispered that the atlas must be inside, perhaps on a table at the top, waiting under the moon. It whispered that its owner might be up there too, just beyond the last curve of the stair. They were wonderful pictures, bright and easy to believe. But she had seen none of it. The windows were dark. The door was closed. Nothing she could see told her what lay behind them. “No,” she said gently, to herself. “That's a guess. A good story, maybe, but still a guess.” She put the pictures down, one at a time, like heavy books she did not need to carry. She stayed there for a long while, walking slowly around the base of the tower, testing the ground, looking up and listening. No voice called down. No light moved in the windows. She found no sign of anyone, no name carved into the stone, no mark that said this belonged to that. And she did not pretend that she had. When she finally stopped, she realized something important had changed. The tower was no longer a mystery shape on the horizon. It was a place she knew, tall and cold and quiet, with eleven dark windows and a closed door. She had gained something real. But the atlas was still unfound, and its owner was still unnamed. She had not learned them. She had only learned where she had not found them, and that was honest knowledge, small and solid. Yasmin gave the stones one last look, then turned back toward the road. The moon had slid a little lower, and the way home looked different from this side, as if the night itself had shifted its shoulders. She walked back slowly, and with each step she turned things over in her mind. The library was waiting for her at the end of the road, a dark shape with a pale roof, exactly where she had left it. When she pushed the great door open again, the familiar smell of paper and wax wrapped around her like a blanket. The moonlight had traveled on while she was gone, and now it lay across the far side of the room, silvering the reading tables and the rail of the gallery. She crossed to the big table and sat down, resting her chin in her hands. She had come back with no answer. But she had come back with something. “Let me say it all out loud,” she told the quiet. “So I don't trick myself.” She counted on her fingers. “I went to the tower. I saw it. It's real, and it's tall, and the door was shut. I didn't find the atlas. I didn't find its owner. I don't know either one.” She paused, listening to the words settle. Then she looked at the next finger. “And the Agreement isn't closed.” There was a tempting thought in the back of her mind, the same one as before: she could call the work done. She could say she had tried, and tried honestly, and that was enough. It would be so easy to write a neat line under everything and go home. But a line drawn over missing facts would be a lie, and she had promised herself she would not tell one, not even a small, tired one. “No,” she said. “It stays open.” She said it firmly, and the library seemed to breathe out around her. The Agreement was hers to carry, and she took it up without grumbling, the way you pick up your own bag. The moonlight crept across the floor and touched the edge of her sleeve. She watched it come, and for the first time that night she was not afraid of it. The Agreement was open. The atlas's owner was unknown. Those two things were still exactly as they had been. But they were no longer a fog. She knew what she had checked and what she had not. She knew the library's corners were searched and the tower was seen. She knew that the next step would begin from here, from this table, with a clear head and a true list of what she did not know. She stood, pushed in her chair, and walked to the shelves. The moonlight went with her, sliding gently along the spines of the books, and Yasmin began again.
